complete_examples.text: The tracks are modeled by finite element method as a ballastless track system widely used in high-speed lines.
As an example, a typical ballastless track system is introduced in the present study.
Generally there are two types of track systems, i.e., ballasted track system and ballastless track system (e.g., slab track system).

The track structures are modelled as a ballastless track including the rail (Euler–Bernoulli beams), the slab track (thin plates), the rail pads (spring-dashpot elements) and the concrete layer (spring-dashpot elements) support-ing the track.
The China high-speed railway ballastless track irregularities average spectrum is adopted to inverse the track irregularities excitation, as seen in Figure 10.
The random track irregularities are inversed via the China high-speed railway ballastless track irregularities average spectrum, as shown in Figure 18.
Temperature load is a vital load type for the ballastless track.
Besides its advantages, the ballastless track has its limitations.

The track is modeled as a ballastless track system, con-sisting of the rail by Bernoulli–Euler beams, track slab by thin-plate elements in general, and the supporting layer by solid elements generally regarded as base plate or base-ment, or equivalently regarded as a mortar layer.
In the TTS dynamic model, the prototype of the train is the CRH2, and that of the ballastless track is the China Railway Track System III (CRTS III).
Due to the periodic structure of the ballastless track, the spatial distribution of CDS also shows periodicity in the longitudinal direction.
As illustrated in Fig. 1, the VTS dynamic interaction is modeled as a rigid-flexible system, which includes the rigid vehicle, the flexible ballastless track and subgrade.
The dynamics parameters of the vehicle, ballastless track and subgrade can be referred to the literature (Zeng et al. 2016; Chen, Sun, and Zhai 2020).

Train-track-subgrade-soil dynamic interaction Ballastless track Interfacial damage Subgrade settlement Track irregularity Finite element modelling A B S T R A C T In this paper, a dynamic model is established to investigate the dynamic behavior of train-track-subgrade-soil (TTSS) interaction.
The main calculational parameters for the high-speed train, ballastless track, and subgrade have been elaborated in Refs. [22,86], here not presented for brevity.
The train-track-bridge dynamic model consists of the high-speed train model, the ballastless track model including rails, track slab, and base plate, and the bridge system.

The typical ballastless track system can be modeled by finite element (FE), in which the rail is modeled by Bernoulli–Euler beam elements, and the track slab and base plate are modeled as plate elements by the Mindlin plate theory.

The original track irregularity (I1) with the wavelength of 0.5–200 m is produced by the ballastless track power spectral density (PSD) of China HSR (PSD of Ballastless Track Irregularities of High-Speed Railway, 2014).
The entire model consists of the rigid vehicle and the flexible ballastless track.
Owing to the ballastless track is a periodicity structure in the longitudinal direction, therefore, the time-domain Green’s function method can be applied to improve the computational efficiency.

Track system can be regarded as a typically layered structure, including the rail, track slab and basement, for the ballastless track, and the rail, sleeper and ballasted bed, for the ballasted track.

In the 2D track model, slab track element, in which two layered Euler beams of the rail and track slab on continuous elastic foundations are adopted as finite element formulations, was developed to analyze the dynamic responses of ballastless track [11].
The main parameters of the ballastless track and soil can be found in Refs [26,28] for reference.
Those results illustrate that the AFZ has a large effect on the mechanical performance of the ballastless track in the vertical direction.

Based on the CRTS I slab ballastless track beam-shell modeling theory, a non-linear spring was used to simulate CA mortar void damage, and the fastener forces were input as the excitation of the model to obtain the vertical acceleration dataset at the monitoring points.
The results show that the beam-shell model reflects the mechanical intricacies of the ballastless track and is feasible for the simulation of the CA mortar void problem.
